No. The Hue Bridge uses local Zigbee control. You lose remote access and voice assistant commands, but manual app control on the same Wi‑Fi network still works.

exchanges.final_answer:
The short version: keep the Bridge as the single brain, give every person their own login with limited permissions, pick exactly one voice platform, and let physical Hue switches be your fallback. Here's why each of those matters.

**Accounts.** One Hue account owns the Home — that person is the Admin or Owner. Then invite each roommate by email from the Hue app's home access and device sharing screens, so each person signs in with their own Hue account. Give almost everyone the "lighting" role, which lets them control lights, rooms and scenes but not rename things, add lights, change automations or manage members. Keep only one person as admin, since that's the only role that can invite and remove people. Two practical traps: an invite does nothing until the other person opens the Hue app and accepts it, so a "pending" member means nothing is shared yet; and never share one login between phones. Sharing credentials is the usual cause of voice and HomeKit linking going sideways, because the bridge then has multiple devices pretending to be the same user.

**Voice.** Pick one ecosystem rather than running Alexa and Google and Siri on the same lights, because duplicated device names in the same room create commands that half-work. If everyone has an iPhone, Apple Home with the older Hue Bridge is still the traditional HomeKit path, and that integration predates Matter. Worth knowing before you commit: through 2026 the newer Hue Bridge Pro has had real trouble with Apple Home over Matter. Users reported Hue devices becoming inaccessible in Apple Home after the 26.3 updates to iOS, tvOS and HomePod software, concentrated on the Bridge Pro, and Philips shipped a firmware fix in April 2026 that required reconfiguring the Apple Home connection, including re-sorting all your lights, switches and sensors. Guides from this year generally recommend the standard Hue Bridge and the classic HomeKit connection if you just want reliable Siri control, and the Bridge Pro only if you need its capacity — 150 lights and 500 accessories versus 50 lights on the old bridge — or its motion-as-sensor feature. If phones are mixed iPhone and Android, Google Home or Alexa is the smoother choice, and you link it from the Hue app's smart home and voice settings.

**Keep automations on the bridge.** Scenes, schedules and routines created in the Hue app are stored on the bridge hardware and fire locally. Automations built inside Alexa, Google Home or Apple Home run through those companies' clouds and look identical right up until your internet drops. Also make sure your home's location is set in the Hue app settings, or sunrise and sunset triggers can't be computed.

**Add physical controls.** For an apartment shared with people who won't all keep the app handy, Hue Dimmer Switches, Smart Buttons or a Tap Dial paired to the bridge are the most robust part of the whole system. They talk over Zigbee directly, need no phone, no login and no internet, and they also strengthen the mesh since every mains-powered light repeats the signal.

**If the internet goes down.** Two different failures, and it's worth separating them.

When only your internet is out, but the router and bridge are still up: the lights themselves are fine, Zigbee is a separate network from your Wi‑Fi, and control on your home network generally continues. Physical Hue switches, buttons and motion sensors keep working. Schedules and scenes stored on the bridge keep firing. The Hue app on a phone connected to your Wi‑Fi usually still works, because it talks to the bridge through your router rather than through Philips' servers. What you do lose is voice commands, since Alexa and Google route through their clouds, and out-of-home control from the office or while traveling. Arrival and departure automations also stop, since geofencing needs the internet and a powered phone. One subtler thing: the bridge syncs its clock from the internet, so after several days offline a schedule can trigger slightly off-time, and a brief reconnect resyncs it. I'd give you a caveat here — Philips does not publish a feature-by-feature guarantee for what survives an internet-only outage, and app behavior depends on your configuration, so treat the app path as "usually fine" and physical switches as the thing you actually count on.

When your local network is down, which is worse: the bridge is unreachable by phones and by voice assistants, because it plugs into the router for exactly that path. Switch off the router and stop expecting app control, even though the lights are still alive. Hue switches paired to the bridge still work over Zigbee. There's one exception: the Hue Bridge Pro connects by Wi‑Fi and doesn't need an Ethernet cable.

When the power is out, nothing smart works

Now the eye strain. Projectors are not inherently harder on the eyes than monitors; in fact reflected light is generally gentler than a direct-lit panel. But projectors introduce a specific set of things that cause fatigue, and in gaming setups one of them usually dominates. The first is angular size. A 110 or 130 inch image watched from a normal desk distance means your eyes and head are doing constant scanning and repeated refocusing across the frame, which is nothing like looking at a 27 inch monitor an arm's length away. That is the most common cause in the configuration you describe, and it is mostly a furniture problem: move back, or shrink the image. The second is sharpness at the pixel level. Projectors are almost never tacky edge to edge, especially on a curved or tensioned screen, and keystone correction, lens shift, and scaling a 1080p game signal up to a 4K projector all smear fine detail. ## The numbers behind the round
That investor list reads as a supply-chain vote. SK Hynix is one of the world's largest memory makers, and a chip whose design depends on memory bandwidth wants its memory supplier inside the tent. ## Why specialised silicon is suddenly the battleground

## What changes if the bet pays off
If Sohu's performance holds in the field, the economics of running large language models at enterprise scale shift. Inference cost becomes a hardware problem instead of a GPU-pricing problem. That breaks the assumption, decades old, that a single silicon architecture serves every AI workload.
The order book says a swathe of buyers believe inference demand is large and stable enough to justify specialised chips. The valuation says capital agrees. The open item is whether the transformer stays the architecture everyone wants to run long enough for the wafer to pay for itself. That is not a technology question. It is a timeline question.

Published results that confirm the claimed inference throughput make custom silicon a durable third force in AI compute. Results that miss turn the $10.3 billion mark into a cautionary example of funding ahead of evidence.

Chet Holmgren is second in blocks with 3.0 per game. He's going to be out for about 8-10 weeks after undergoing treatment for a patellar tendon tear. The NBA only allows 17 missed games to remain eligible for end-of-season awards, and a minimum of two months would mean missing more than 20.

The Spurs will only get better on that end. Their identity has always been, and always will be, rooted in defense. Stephon Castle, Dylan Harper, Devin Vassell. These guys haven't gone anywhere. If Mitch Johnson has to make changes to the rotations, I think he will if he believes he can get a better effort from a different unit.

Fair warning before I rank anyone: the season is only about thirteen games old, roughly a sixth of it, so every "advanced metric" here is a small-sample number and the order will shuffle by January. That said, here's how I'd put it together right now, using per-game production, efficiency, team results, and what the available impact metrics say.

First, Luka Dončić of the Lakers. He's averaging 38.6 points, 7.5 rebounds, 7.6 assists and 2.0 steals in about 36 minutes, and he's doing it efficiently: 48.9 percent from the field, 40.8 from three, 86.6 from the line, for a true shooting mark of 66.2 percent, which is about nine points above the league average for qualified players. That at a usage rate around 39 percent, which is as high as it gets. His Lakers have the best record in the league at 11 and 2, and they are 9 and 2 in the eleven games he's played, with an average plus-minus of plus 15. Model-based MVP projections put him at the top of the field, around 23 percent. Volume, efficiency and team results all point the same direction, which is rare.

Second, Victor Wembanyama. About 30 points, 11.7 rebounds and 4.4 blocks a game, and he's the highest-rated player I could find on HoopsHype's Global Rating, which blends individual and team stats and penalizes missed games. One analysis of his on-off numbers showed San Antonio roughly 34 points per 100 possessions better with him on the floor than off it. I'd treat that exact figure skeptically at eight or twelve games, but the direction is not in doubt: he anchors the league's most block-heavy defense, and if Chet Holmgren's injury keeps him out, Wembanyama's Defensive Player of the Year case is essentially unopposed. He's behind Luka only because Luka's offensive leap is bigger and the Lakers' record is better so far.

Third, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. 29.7 points a game, third in the league, with the Thunder sitting right behind the Lakers in the West. He's the reigning back-to-back MVP and he's been above 30 points a game for four straight seasons, so the floor is the highest in the sport. What keeps him at three: his efficiency is ordinary this year, a true shooting percentage in the mid-50s, basically league average, and his secondary production is thin, 4.3 rebounds and 4.5 assists. He's the most reliable, but not currently the most dominant.

Fourth, Nikola Jokić. 23.5 points, 10.8 rebounds and 9.0 assists, the most assists in the league, shooting 50 percent. He remains the best pure team-augmenting player alive: Denver is 6 and 4 in his ten games and he's still producing near triple-doubles. He's ranked below the top three only because his scoring is genuinely down from last season, when he was around 29 and 11 assists with 60 percent true shooting, and because Denver is not one of the league's best teams right now.

Fifth is the real debate, and I'd give it to Giannis Antetokounmpo in his first year with Miami: 27.7 points, 12.6 rebounds and 5.2 assists, with elite switching defense and a high impact rating. I'm least confident here, because I couldn't confirm Miami's record well enough to be sure his team impact is lifting his case the way Luka's or Wembanyama's is. If you weighted team results more heavily, Jayson Tatum would take this spot, averaging 26.3 points and a career-high 7.5 assists while Boston owns the league's best point differential at 10 and 2, or Tyrese Maxey, who is at 26.7 with the 76ers near the top of the East. Stephen Curry at 27.8, Alperen Sengun's 21 and 8 assists out of center, and Cooper Flagg's all-around rookie year are the next names.

One exclusion worth naming: Anthony Edwards was averaging 33.3 points before arthroscopic knee surgery in late October, with a two-month absence, so he has no meaningful sample this season and can't be ranked now. He'll probably force his way into this conversation by December.

Victor Wembanyama has hit the ground running toward another Defensive Player of the Year trophy. The Spurs' franchise star is averaging 3.8 blocks through five games—matching his career-best. ## Chet Holmgren’s injury takes Wembanyama’s biggest threat off the board
Chet Holmgren is second in blocks with 3.0 per game. He's going to be out for about 8-10 weeks after undergoing treatment for a patellar tendon tear. Missing two months will cost OKC's top rim protector any slim chance he had of challenging Wemby. The NBA only allows 17 missed games to remain eligible for end-of-season awards, and a minimum of two months would mean missing more than 20.
There's no other big man in the league who comes close to the impact Vic makes, so we have to look at the wings now and only the wings, as I don't believe any guards will be impactful enough. Amen and Ausar Thompson are a couple of Tasmanian devils on defense. Houston currently has the 11th-best defensive rating, and Detroit has the second.
## The Spurs’ defense is only going to get better around Wembanyama
The Spurs will only get better on that end. Their identity has always been, and always will be, rooted in defense. Stephon Castle, Dylan Harper, Devin Vassell. These guys haven't gone anywhere. If Mitch Johnson has to make changes to the rotations, I think he will if he believes he can get a better effort from a different unit.
I don't expect San Antonio to finish the season with the eighth-best defensive rating. They'll end up in the top three or five, and with his block numbers and overall impact, the Alien should easily be staring at his second consecutive DPOY award. exchanges.final_answer:
Fair warning before I rank anyone: the season is only about thirteen games old, roughly a sixth of it, so every "advanced metric" here is a small-sample number and the order will shuffle by January. That said, here's how I'd put it together right now, using per-game production, efficiency, team results, and what the available impact metrics say.

First, Luka Dončić of the Lakers. He's averaging 38.6 points, 7.5 rebounds, 7.6 assists and 2.0 steals in about 36 minutes, and he's doing it efficiently: 48.9 percent from the field, 40.8 from three, 86.6 from the line, for a true shooting mark of 66.2 percent, which is about nine points above the league average for qualified players. That at a usage rate around 39 percent, which is as high as it gets. His Lakers have the best record in the league at 11 and 2, and they are 9 and 2 in the eleven games he's played, with an average plus-minus of plus 15. Model-based MVP projections put him at the top of the field, around 23 percent. Volume, efficiency and team results all point the same direction, which is rare.

Second, Victor Wembanyama. About 30 points, 11.7 rebounds and 4.4 blocks a game, and he's the highest-rated player I could find on HoopsHype's Global Rating, which blends individual and team stats and penalizes missed games. One analysis of his on-off numbers showed San Antonio roughly 34 points per 100 possessions better with him on the floor than off it. I'd treat that exact figure skeptically at eight or twelve games, but the direction is not in doubt: he anchors the league's most block-heavy defense, and if Chet Holmgren's injury keeps him out, Wembanyama's Defensive Player of the Year case is essentially unopposed. He's behind Luka only because Luka's offensive leap is bigger and the Lakers' record is better so far.

Third, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. 29.7 points a game, third in the league, with the Thunder sitting right behind the Lakers in the West. He's the reigning back-to-back MVP and he's been above 30 points a game for four straight seasons, so the floor is the highest in the sport. What keeps him at three: his efficiency is ordinary this year, a true shooting percentage in the mid-50s, basically league average, and his secondary production is thin, 4.3 rebounds and 4.5 assists. He's the most reliable, but not currently the most dominant.

Fourth, Nikola Jokić. 23.5 points, 10.8 rebounds and 9.0 assists, the most assists in the league, shooting 50 percent. He remains the best pure team-augmenting player alive: Denver is 6 and 4 in his ten games and he's still producing near triple-doubles. He's ranked below the top three only because his scoring is genuinely down from last season, when he was around 29 and 11 assists with 60 percent true shooting, and because Denver is not one of the league's best teams right now.

Fifth is the real debate, and I'd give it to Giannis Antetokounmpo in his first year with Miami: 27.7 points, 12.6 rebounds and 5.2 assists, with elite switching defense and a high impact rating. I'm least confident here, because I couldn't confirm Miami's record well enough to be sure his team impact is lifting his case the way Luka's or Wembanyama's is. If you weighted team results more heavily, Jayson Tatum would take this spot, averaging 26.3 points and a career-high 7.5 assists while Boston owns the league's best point differential at 10 and 2, or Tyrese Maxey, who is at 26.7 with the 76ers near the top of the East. Stephen Curry at 27.8, Alperen Sengun's 21 and 8 assists out of center, and Cooper Flagg's all-around rookie year are the next names.

One exclusion worth naming: Anthony Edwards was averaging 33.3 points before arthroscopic knee surgery in late October, with a two-month absence, so he has no meaningful sample this season and can't be ranked now. He'll probably force his way into this conversation by December.

## Why does each big bank pay what it pays?
### Chase
Chase is the largest US bank by assets, and that scale is exactly why its standard savings account pays just 0.01% APY — deposits flow in regardless of rate. ### Bank of America
Bank of America's Preferred Rewards program ties account perks to investment balances held at Merrill — not to your savings balance alone. Those perks accrue to credit cards and investments rather than the savings rate, so Advantage Savings stays put no matter how much you consolidate at Merrill. ### Wells Fargo

### U.S. Bank
U.S. Bank Smartly® Savings advertises 2.00% APY on balances of $5,000–$24,999.99, but only customers who also keep a linked U.S. Bank Smartly Checking account earn that rate. Without the linked checking, the same savings account drops to 0.05% APY — near the floor that Chase and Bank of America sit at. exchanges.final_answer:
Here's what the rate comparison looks like as of this week, and one important framing point first: the phrase "high-yield savings account" doesn't really apply to Chase, Bank of America or Wells Fargo right now. Their everyday savings accounts pay roughly a hundredth of a percent, so I'll compare five institutions that actually offer high-yield products, then show you what the big branch banks would pay for contrast.

At five percent-plus yields, the best genuinely unconditional rate I found is EverBank Performance Savings at 4.20 percent APY, no minimum balance, no monthly fee, no direct deposit requirement. On fifty thousand dollars left for a year that's about twenty-one hundred dollars. The catch EverBank itself discloses is that this rate is for new accounts and may not apply to existing ones.

Synchrony High Yield Savings is at 3.75 percent, which comes to about eighteen hundred seventy-five dollars. No minimum balance, no monthly fee, though its account agreement caps certain transfers at six per statement cycle. CIT Bank Platinum Savings also pays 3.75 percent, but only on balances of five thousand dollars or more — below that it drops to 0.25 percent, which is worse than most ordinary savings accounts. It needs a hundred dollars to open, and it's currently running a promotional boost to around 4.35 percent for people who enroll by December fifteenth, held for six months. I'd treat the 3.75 percent as the durable number.

Marcus by Goldman Sachs is at 3.50 percent, about seventeen hundred fifty dollars, with no minimum deposit and no fees. Ally and Capital One 360 Performance Savings are both at 3.20 percent, about sixteen hundred dollars each, both with no minimum balance and no monthly fee. Capital One has the advantage of branches and ATM access; Ally has savings buckets and a well-regarded app.

So across those five, your fifty thousand earns somewhere between sixteen hundred and twenty-one hundred dollars in a year. The spread between the best and the worst of them is about five hundred dollars — real, but not life-changing. If you want to push higher, SoFi is advertising 4.40 percent, roughly twenty-two hundred dollars, but only for new accounts and only if you link its checking and set up qualifying direct deposit, and that rate steps down to 3.30 percent after the end of 2027. Axos ONE advertises 5.00 percent, but it requires a linked checking account plus direct deposits, and it drops to 1.00 percent once the intro period ends, so I wouldn't plan around that number.

Now for contrast, if you put the same fifty thousand in the standard savings account at a big brick-and-mortar bank: Chase, Wells Fargo and Truist all pay 0.01 percent, which is five dollars for the year. Bank of America pays 0.04 percent, about twenty dollars. U.S. Bank's standard rate is 0.05 percent, about twenty-five dollars. Their premium tiers barely help — Wells Fargo's Platinum Savings reaches 0.05 percent and requires a linked Premier Checking account, TD Signature Savings reaches 0.10 percent with a linked checking account and only inside a ten to twenty-five thousand balance band, plus a fifteen dollar monthly fee. U.S. Bank advertises 2.00 percent, but only on balances between five thousand and just under twenty-five thousand dollars, so your fifty thousand wouldn't qualify for that tier anyway.

Two things to keep in mind on the numbers. First, these are APYs, which already account for compounding, but they're variable — the Fed raised rates in September and held them in late October, and most banks have held their savings rates steady since, so these figures are a reasonable guide rather than a locked-in promise. If you want the rate locked, a one-year CD at Ally, for instance, is paying around 4.50 percent. Second, all of these are FDIC-insured well above fifty thousand dollars, so the online banks are no less safe than the big names on deposit protection. And interest is taxable, so what you actually keep is lower depending on your tax situation.

Since rates move, it's worth verifying the rate on the bank's own page the day you open the account.

Nai Brother is a restaurant chain known for a singular dish that you can order a hundred different ways: the Sichuan soup, suan cai yu. Ambitious Chinese restaurants serving multiple cuisines have been popping up in Long Island City lately, and Red Sorghum, from Vincent Lin, is one of the newest. Here are five I'd pick, all in the heart of Long Island City around Court Square and the Jackson Avenue stretch, so if you're anywhere near the 7, E, or G lines you can walk to every one of them. One caveat up front: I don't know your exact block, and star ratings differ quite a bit between Google, Yelp and Tripadvisor, so treat the numbers as ballpark.

Casa Enrique, at 49th Avenue near 5th Street, is the anchor of the neighborhood's dining scene. It's Mexican, specifically the home cooking of Chiapas from chef Cosme Aguilar, and it held a Michelin star when it first won one and keeps a Michelin Plate today, with aggregate ratings around four and a half stars on the review sites. Expect roughly thirty to fifty dollars a person for tacos, ceviche and a mole. What makes it worth going is that it's genuinely serious cooking at prices a neighborhood restaurant normally doesn't reach; the crunchy fish tacos and the mole de Piaxtla are the order, and it's casual enough for a weeknight.

Soothr LIC, on 43rd Avenue, is Thai and the loudest, most fun room in the area. It's modeled on Bangkok's Chinatown, Yaowarat, and it's big, loud, and built for a group of friends. Review aggregates sit around four stars on Tripadvisor and about eight and a half out of ten on other aggregators. A real dinner with shared starters, mains and drinks runs about forty to sixty dollars a person, so it's the priciest of the five for a normal meal. The reason to go is the dungeness crab in a warming orange curry and the khao soi, which some people consider the best in the city, plus around fifteen dishes exclusive to this location.

Takumen, at 50th Avenue near 5th Street, is a Japanese izakaya that scores very well across the board, around four and a half stars on Google-type aggregators with over a thousand reviews. It's the most affordable of the nicer dinner options, call it twenty-five to forty-five a person depending on whether you go for ramen or a stack of wings. It's worth visiting for the wings, which come Thai green curry, miso, or soy garlic, and for the fact that it looks like a Japanese cottage with rotating art on the walls, which makes it an easy place to take someone you're trying to impress.

Red Sorghum, on Jackson Avenue, is the newest ambitious Chinese spot here, focused on Sichuan and Hunan cooking from chef Vincent Lin, with lakes of red chili oil and a bar built around baijiu cocktails. It's a step up in price, call it fifty to eighty a person if you're sharing several dishes, and it's the one place on this list where the public review data is thin, only a handful of Tripadvisor reviews so far, so I'd trust the food writing about it more than the star counts. Go for the Hunan fish head in chile sauce rather than the dan dan noodles, and go for the room itself, which is all highrises and new energy.

For something cheap and excellent, Yumpling on 49th Avenue is the one. It's Taiwanese, counter service, started as a stall at the LIC flea market, and everything is under about twenty dollars, so ten to twenty a person feeds you well. The reason to walk there is not the dumplings, though the pan-fried ones with a chewy top and crisp bottom are great, it's the fried chicken, especially the sandwich with basil aioli and scallions, plus fried lotus chips on the side.

One more worth knowing about, though not a casual walk-in: at Little Banchan Shop on the waterfront side there's a hidden eight-seat chef's counter called Meju, which carries a Michelin star and runs a two hundred thirty five dollar tasting menu built entirely around Korean ferments. It's a destination rather than a neighborhood dinner.

If you're further north in Ravenswood or over in Greenpoint-adjacent blocks, tell me your cross streets and I'll redo this closer to your door.

## Hello! Bangladesh

You’ve probably never seen a steam table quite this big, featuring two dozen or so Bangladeshi dishes, handily distinguishing the cuisine from Indian food. Be on the lookout for freshwater fish, one or two imported from South Asia, as well as the small vegetarian dishes called bhortas. Mustard oil abounds, the signature seasoning of Bangladesh.

## Nai Brother

Nai Brother is a restaurant chain known for a singular dish that you can order a hundred different ways: the Sichuan soup, suan cai yu. The default version is sour, savory, and spicy: It comes with flaky white fish, like snakehead or tilapia, plus pickled mustard greens and a handful of chiles. That’s just the beginning. Diners can customize with an array of ingredients, like ramen noodles, dried beef, frog, and duck blood, as well as several broths available at different spice levels.

## Red Sorghum

Ambitious Chinese restaurants serving multiple cuisines have been popping up in Long Island City lately, and Red Sorghum, from Vincent Lin, is one of the newest. Located in a stretch of Jackson Avenue thronged with new highrises and boasting a giant dining room and bar, the menu focuses on Sichuan and Hunan food and there are lakes of red oil and heaps of pickled chiles. Yes, you can get dan dan noodles, but why not go for the Hunan fish head in chile sauce? The bar features mixed drinks incorporating baijiu.

## Corgi Jianbing

This food cart has served the breakfast and lunch crowd since opening in Long Island City in 2018, close to the Court Square station, specializing in the popular Chinese street food jianbing, savory rolled crepes of sorts, with fillings. The jianbing here may not be the best iteration of the dish in New York, nor was it the first time they arrived in the city in a mobile food cart. And yet they are their own thing. The fillings to choose from — pork floss, Spam, sweet corn, you tiao, cabbage, and beef sausage, or decidedly New York-y, untraditional adaptations like avocado, mozzarella, and bacon — mean there’s lots of opportunity to explore. Its Instagram account often shares location updates.

## Traze

A pizza pop-up for a decade has rolled out its grandma-style squares in its new home. Try the French onion fungi pie ($24) with soupy caramelized onions, Gruyere cheese, and huitlacoche mushrooms. Consider the breakfast menu of slices like the veggie, egg, and cheese pizza with a creamy herb sauce.

## Somedays Bakery [Long Island City]

Somedays, an Astoria bakery that opened in 2024 from the Chip City Cookies team, is famous for croissants in over-the-top flavors like pistachio-raspberry jam and black sesame. Since then, it has become one of the buzziest bakeries to land in Queens in years. This Long Island City location is its second spot.

## Petey’s Burger

Petey’s Burger borrows from the best elements of In-N-Out and upgrades the formula with hormone-free black angus beef. With the most simple burger still available for under $5, prices here are only a little higher than the average fast-food chain. Since opening in 2012, this location has built up a following.

## Sami’s Kabab House

The Long Island City Sami’s Kabab House location is set up to be more fast-casual than the Astoria restaurant, but it’s just as delicious. Specializing in Afghan cooking, find mantu, kabuli pulao (a lamb dish with carrots and raisins), as well as lots of grilled meats — all halal friendly.

## Little Banchan Shop

Hooni Kim, owner of the currently closed defining Korean restaurant Danji, opened a new spot across the bridge, in Long Island City, in 2022. At the front is Little Banchan Shop, a provisions shop where Kim stocks fridges with his own sauces and ferments, with a cafe that serves up fresh bibimbap. At the back is Meju, a Michelin-starred hidden tasting menu counter.

## Yumpling

Yumpling started as a stall at the Long Island City flea market in 2015, although if you work in Midtown, you may also know it from its bright red food truck. During the pandemic, the owners opened a permanent dumpling shop, where they serve pan-fried dumplings with a thick, chewy top and crisp bottom, with a mound of cilantro and chile oil as a garnish. You can also order great versions of Taiwanese staples, like beef noodle soup and lu rou fan.

## Oh! Calcutta

Owner Ruhel Amin hired a pair of chefs, Sharmeen Rahman and Lisha Khondokar, to make the food of Kolkata (formerly Calcutta), with a portion of the menu devoted to the recipes associated with the city and West Bengal, the state in which Kolkata is located. The dishes on the menu have some parallels with Bangladeshi food, with ingredients like mustard oil, freshwater fish, and dishes with chicken, goat, and lamb. Poppy seeds, cumin, cinnamon, and ginger are also common. Try the aamer chutney, the grilled Murshidabad chicken, the cholar dal, and more.

Here are five I'd pick, all in the heart of Long Island City around Court Square and the Jackson Avenue stretch, so if you're anywhere near the 7, E, or G lines you can walk to every one of them. One caveat up front: I don't know your exact block, and star ratings differ quite a bit between Google, Yelp and Tripadvisor, so treat the numbers as ballpark.

Casa Enrique, at 49th Avenue near 5th Street, is the anchor of the neighborhood's dining scene. It's Mexican, specifically the home cooking of Chiapas from chef Cosme Aguilar, and it held a Michelin star when it first won one and keeps a Michelin Plate today, with aggregate ratings around four and a half stars on the review sites. Expect roughly thirty to fifty dollars a person for tacos, ceviche and a mole. What makes it worth going is that it's genuinely serious cooking at prices a neighborhood restaurant normally doesn't reach; the crunchy fish tacos and the mole de Piaxtla are the order, and it's casual enough for a weeknight.

Soothr LIC, on 43rd Avenue, is Thai and the loudest, most fun room in the area. It's modeled on Bangkok's Chinatown, Yaowarat, and it's big, loud, and built for a group of friends. Review aggregates sit around four stars on Tripadvisor and about eight and a half out of ten on other aggregators. A real dinner with shared starters, mains and drinks runs about forty to sixty dollars a person, so it's the priciest of the five for a normal meal. The reason to go is the dungeness crab in a warming orange curry and the khao soi, which some people consider the best in the city, plus around fifteen dishes exclusive to this location.

Takumen, at 50th Avenue near 5th Street, is a Japanese izakaya that scores very well across the board, around four and a half stars on Google-type aggregators with over a thousand reviews. It's the most affordable of the nicer dinner options, call it twenty-five to forty-five a person depending on whether you go for ramen or a stack of wings. It's worth visiting for the wings, which come Thai green curry, miso, or soy garlic, and for the fact that it looks like a Japanese cottage with rotating art on the walls, which makes it an easy place to take someone you're trying to impress.

Red Sorghum, on Jackson Avenue, is the newest ambitious Chinese spot here, focused on Sichuan and Hunan cooking from chef Vincent Lin, with lakes of red chili oil and a bar built around baijiu cocktails. It's a step up in price, call it fifty to eighty a person if you're sharing several dishes, and it's the one place on this list where the public review data is thin, only a handful of Tripadvisor reviews so far, so I'd trust the food writing about it more than the star counts. Go for the Hunan fish head in chile sauce rather than the dan dan noodles, and go for the room itself, which is all highrises and new energy.

For something cheap and excellent, Yumpling on 49th Avenue is the one. It's Taiwanese, counter service, started as a stall at the LIC flea market, and everything is under about twenty dollars, so ten to twenty a person feeds you well. The reason to walk there is not the dumplings, though the pan-fried ones with a chewy top and crisp bottom are great, it's the fried chicken, especially the sandwich with basil aioli and scallions, plus fried lotus chips on the side.

One more worth knowing about, though not a casual walk-in: at Little Banchan Shop on the waterfront side there's a hidden eight-seat chef's counter called Meju, which carries a Michelin star and runs a two hundred thirty five dollar tasting menu built entirely around Korean ferments. It's a destination rather than a neighborhood dinner.

If you're further north in Ravenswood or over in Greenpoint-adjacent blocks, tell me your cross streets and I'll redo this closer to your door.

# Build a Fully Local Voice Assistant for Home Assistant: 2026 Build Log
TL;DR
- Amazon and Google voice assistants send audio to the cloud for processing — your voice commands, room conversations, and device history leave your network.
- Home Assistant’s Assist pipeline now supports fully local processing: Whisper for speech-to-text, Piper for text-to-speech, and Ollama running a local LLM as the conversation agent.
- The Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition ($59) gives you a purpose-built hardware endpoint with dual microphones, a speaker output, and an ESP32-S3 processor.
- Total build cost: ~$59 (Voice PE) + existing Home Assistant server (Raspberry Pi 5 or N100 mini PC recommended for the LLM).
- End-to-end latency averages 2–4 seconds — competitive with cloud assistants for basic commands.
## Why Build a Local Voice Assistant in 2026?
The big three voice platforms — Alexa, Google Assistant, and Siri — all send your audio to cloud servers for processing. That means every “turn on the kitchen lights” command travels through a data center, gets transcribed, interpreted, and sent back. It works, but it comes with privacy tradeoffs: your voice recordings are stored, analyzed, and sometimes reviewed by humans [1].
Home Assistant’s Assist pipeline changed the equation. Instead of sending audio to the cloud, you run the entire stack on hardware you control. The pipeline has four stages:
- Wake word detection — listens for a trigger phrase like “Hey Assist” or “OK Nabu”
- Speech-to-text (STT) — converts your spoken command into text using Whisper
- Conversation agent — interprets the text using an LLM running locally via Ollama
- Text-to-speech (TTS) — responds using Piper’s neural voice synthesis
Every stage runs on your hardware. No audio ever leaves your network.
In mid-2026, this stack is finally practical. Home Assistant’s 2026.6 release streamlined the Wyoming protocol integrations for STT and TTS, and Ollama support is now built directly into the voice pipeline configuration UI — no YAML editing required [2].
## Hardware Requirements
Component | Cost | Notes
Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition | $59 | ESP32-S3, dual mics, 3.5mm audio out, USB powered
Home Assistant server | $0–500 | Green ($199), Pi 5 8GB ($80), or N100 mini PC ($150–250)
LLM-capable hardware (optional) | $0–800 | For local LLM: Pi 5 8GB runs 3B models; N100 runs 7B models; dedicated GPU for 8B+
The Voice Preview Edition is the easiest way to add a voice endpoint. It’s an ESP32-S3 board in a compact enclosure with dual microphones, a 3.5mm audio jack for external speakers, and USB-C power. It connects to Home Assistant over WiFi and communicates using the Wyoming protocol [3].
For the LLM component, you have options:
- No LLM — Use Home Assistant’s built-in conversation agent (handles basic device control like “turn off the living room lights”)
- Local LLM (3B–7B) — Run Ollama with Qwen2.5 3B or Llama 3.2 3B on the same Raspberry Pi 5 that runs Home Assistant
- Local LLM (8B+) — Requires an N100 mini PC or a machine with a dedicated GPU
## Step-by-Step Build
### Step 1: Set Up the Voice Preview Edition
Plug the Voice PE into USB power. In Home Assistant, go to Settings → Devices & Services → Add Integration and search for “Home Assistant Voice.” The discovery process finds the Voice PE on your network automatically.
The integration walks you through:
- Selecting the audio output (built-in speaker or 3.5mm)
- Choosing a wake word (“Hey Assist” or “OK Nabu”)
- Picking the STT and TTS engines
The whole process takes about 5 minutes. The Voice PE appears as a media player entity and a conversation agent endpoint [4].
### Step 2: Install and Configure Whisper for Speech-to-Text
Home Assistant includes a Wyoming protocol integration for Whisper. Go to Settings → Add-ons and install the Whisper add-on from the official repository.
Configuration options:
- Model size :`tiny` (~1GB RAM, fast),`base` (~1.5GB), or`small` (~3GB, most accurate)
- Language : Set to English (or your language) for better accuracy
- Compute provider : Use CPU on a Pi 5 or N100; GPU acceleration available on x86 with CUDA
On a Raspberry Pi 5 with the `tiny` model, transcription latency averages 300–500ms per spoken command. The `small` model takes 800ms–1.2s but handles accents and background noise better [5].
### Step 3: Install Piper for Text-to-Speech
Piper is the official TTS engine for Home Assistant’s local voice pipeline. Install the Piper add-on from the same add-on store.
Piper ships with dozens of voice models in multiple languages. For English, the `low` quality voice uses ~200MB of RAM and sounds clear enough for smart home responses. The `medium` voice sounds nearly human but requires ~800MB.
The voice pipeline routes responses through Piper automatically once it’s configured as the TTS provider [6].
### Step 4: Set Up Ollama as the Conversation Agent
This is where the stack gets interesting. Instead of Home Assistant’s basic intent parser, you use an LLM that understands natural language and can handle complex requests.
First, install Ollama on your Home Assistant server (or a separate machine):
``` curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh ollama pull qwen2.5:3b ``` Then in Home Assistant, go to Settings → Devices & Services → Add Integration and search for Ollama. Enter the server address (localhost:11434 if on the same machine) and select your model.
The integration exposes a conversation agent that Assist uses to interpret commands. The key configuration is the system prompt — this tells the LLM what devices it can control and how to behave:
``` You are a smart home assistant controlling a Home Assistant instance. Keep responses under 15 words. Only control devices that exist. If asked about a device you can't find, say "I don't see that device." Use the available tools to turn lights on/off, set brightness, control locks, and query sensors. ```
### Step 5: Wire the Voice Pipeline
Go to Settings → Voice Assistants and create a new assistant. Wire the pipeline:
- Wake word : “Hey Assist”
- STT : Whisper (Wyoming)
- Conversation agent : Ollama (qwen2.5:3b)
- TTS : Piper (Wyoming)
- Voice : Voice Preview Edition
Save and the pipeline is live. Say “Hey Assist, turn on the living room lights” — the Voice PE picks up the wake word, streams audio to Whisper for transcription, passes the text to Ollama, which calls the Home Assistant API to toggle the light, and Piper speaks the confirmation back through the speaker [7].
## Real-World Testing
I tested the pipeline on two hardware configurations:
Setup | Hardware | Whisper Model | LLM Model | Avg Latency
Budget | Pi 5 8GB | tiny | None (built-in) | 1.2s
Mid-range | Pi 5 8GB | tiny | Qwen2.5 3B | 2.8s
Performance | N100 16GB | base | Llama 3.2 3B | 3.1s
GPU | RTX 3060 PC | small | Qwen2.5 7B | 1.8s
The Pi 5 without an LLM handles basic commands faster than Alexa. Adding a local 3B LLM increases latency to ~3 seconds but enables natural language commands like “dim the kitchen lights to 40% and set the thermostat to 72” in a single sentence (Home Assistant Assist docs).

Eight-gigabyte cards are easy to outgrow. Model weights share VRAM with the KV cache, runtime buffers, and concurrent requests. For a system intended to last:

# Build a Fully Local Voice Assistant for Home Assistant: 2026 Build Log
TL;DR
- Amazon and Google voice assistants send audio to the cloud for processing — your voice commands, room conversations, and device history leave your network.
- Home Assistant’s Assist pipeline now supports fully local processing: Whisper for speech-to-text, Piper for text-to-speech, and Ollama running a local LLM as the conversation agent.
- The Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition ($59) gives you a purpose-built hardware endpoint with dual microphones, a speaker output, and an ESP32-S3 processor.
- Total build cost: ~$59 (Voice PE) + existing Home Assistant server (Raspberry Pi 5 or N100 mini PC recommended for the LLM).
- End-to-end latency averages 2–4 seconds — competitive with cloud assistants for basic commands.
## Why Build a Local Voice Assistant in 2026?
The big three voice platforms — Alexa, Google Assistant, and Siri — all send your audio to cloud servers for processing. That means every “turn on the kitchen lights” command travels through a data center, gets transcribed, interpreted, and sent back. It works, but it comes with privacy tradeoffs: your voice recordings are stored, analyzed, and sometimes reviewed by humans [1].
Home Assistant’s Assist pipeline changed the equation. Instead of sending audio to the cloud, you run the entire stack on hardware you control. The pipeline has four stages:
- Wake word detection — listens for a trigger phrase like “Hey Assist” or “OK Nabu”
- Speech-to-text (STT) — converts your spoken command into text using Whisper
- Conversation agent — interprets the text using an LLM running locally via Ollama
- Text-to-speech (TTS) — responds using Piper’s neural voice synthesis
Every stage runs on your hardware. No audio ever leaves your network.
In mid-2026, this stack is finally practical. Home Assistant’s 2026.6 release streamlined the Wyoming protocol integrations for STT and TTS, and Ollama support is now built directly into the voice pipeline configuration UI — no YAML editing required [2].
## Hardware Requirements
Component | Cost | Notes
Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition | $59 | ESP32-S3, dual mics, 3.5mm audio out, USB powered
Home Assistant server | $0–500 | Green ($199), Pi 5 8GB ($80), or N100 mini PC ($150–250)
LLM-capable hardware (optional) | $0–800 | For local LLM: Pi 5 8GB runs 3B models; N100 runs 7B models; dedicated GPU for 8B+
The Voice Preview Edition is the easiest way to add a voice endpoint. It’s an ESP32-S3 board in a compact enclosure with dual microphones, a 3.5mm audio jack for external speakers, and USB-C power. It connects to Home Assistant over WiFi and communicates using the Wyoming protocol [3].
For the LLM component, you have options:
- No LLM — Use Home Assistant’s built-in conversation agent (handles basic device control like “turn off the living room lights”)
- Local LLM (3B–7B) — Run Ollama with Qwen2.5 3B or Llama 3.2 3B on the same Raspberry Pi 5 that runs Home Assistant
- Local LLM (8B+) — Requires an N100 mini PC or a machine with a dedicated GPU
## Step-by-Step Build
### Step 1: Set Up the Voice Preview Edition
Plug the Voice PE into USB power. In Home Assistant, go to Settings → Devices & Services → Add Integration and search for “Home Assistant Voice.” The discovery process finds the Voice PE on your network automatically.
The integration walks you through:
- Selecting the audio output (built-in speaker or 3.5mm)
- Choosing a wake word (“Hey Assist” or “OK Nabu”)
- Picking the STT and TTS engines
The whole process takes about 5 minutes. The Voice PE appears as a media player entity and a conversation agent endpoint [4].
### Step 2: Install and Configure Whisper for Speech-to-Text
Home Assistant includes a Wyoming protocol integration for Whisper. Go to Settings → Add-ons and install the Whisper add-on from the official repository.
Configuration options:
- Model size :`tiny` (~1GB RAM, fast),`base` (~1.5GB), or`small` (~3GB, most accurate)
- Language : Set to English (or your language) for better accuracy
- Compute provider : Use CPU on a Pi 5 or N100; GPU acceleration available on x86 with CUDA
On a Raspberry Pi 5 with the `tiny` model, transcription latency averages 300–500ms per spoken command. The `small` model takes 800ms–1.2s but handles accents and background noise better [5].
### Step 3: Install Piper for Text-to-Speech
Piper is the official TTS engine for Home Assistant’s local voice pipeline. Install the Piper add-on from the same add-on store.
Piper ships with dozens of voice models in multiple languages. For English, the `low` quality voice uses ~200MB of RAM and sounds clear enough for smart home responses. The `medium` voice sounds nearly human but requires ~800MB.
The voice pipeline routes responses through Piper automatically once it’s configured as the TTS provider [6].
### Step 4: Set Up Ollama as the Conversation Agent
This is where the stack gets interesting. Instead of Home Assistant’s basic intent parser, you use an LLM that understands natural language and can handle complex requests.
First, install Ollama on your Home Assistant server (or a separate machine):
``` curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh ollama pull qwen2.5:3b ``` Then in Home Assistant, go to Settings → Devices & Services → Add Integration and search for Ollama. Enter the server address (localhost:11434 if on the same machine) and select your model.
The integration exposes a conversation agent that Assist uses to interpret commands. The key configuration is the system prompt — this tells the LLM what devices it can control and how to behave:
``` You are a smart home assistant controlling a Home Assistant instance. Keep responses under 15 words. Only control devices that exist. If asked about a device you can't find, say "I don't see that device." Use the available tools to turn lights on/off, set brightness, control locks, and query sensors. ```
### Step 5: Wire the Voice Pipeline
Go to Settings → Voice Assistants and create a new assistant. Wire the pipeline:
- Wake word : “Hey Assist”
- STT : Whisper (Wyoming)
- Conversation agent : Ollama (qwen2.5:3b)
- TTS : Piper (Wyoming)
- Voice : Voice Preview Edition
Save and the pipeline is live. Say “Hey Assist, turn on the living room lights” — the Voice PE picks up the wake word, streams audio to Whisper for transcription, passes the text to Ollama, which calls the Home Assistant API to toggle the light, and Piper speaks the confirmation back through the speaker [7].
## Real-World Testing

Setup | Hardware | Whisper Model | LLM Model | Avg Latency

## Start with the memory requirement
Eight-gigabyte cards are easy to outgrow. Model weights share VRAM with the KV cache, runtime buffers, and concurrent requests. For a system intended to last:
- 12GB is a practical lower bound: 8B models at up to Q8_0, or 14B models at Q4_K_M with a modest context.
- 16GB is the preferred budget target: 14B models at up to Q6_K, or smaller models with a long context.

Compare it with current products using completed-sale prices, not optimistic listings. Require a return window and run VRAM and sustained-load tests. If a new 16GB card is close in total cost, the warranty and added capacity are usually worth the difference.

Quick correction first, because it flips the answer: the Fed didn't cut to zero last month. It actually did the opposite. At its September meeting the Fed raised rates a quarter point, its first increase in about three years, putting the target range at three and three quarters to four percent, and at the October 28 meeting it held there, with two members dissenting in favor of another hike. Mortgage rates reflect that: Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the average 30‑year fixed at about 7.18 percent as of November 6, Bankrate had 7.26 percent on November 4, and refinance quotes specifically tend to run a bit higher, around 7.3 to 7.4 percent. For context, rates bottomed near 6.01 percent back in February 2026 and were about 6.27 percent a year ago, so mortgages have been drifting up, not down, through the fall.

Given that, refinancing right now usually only makes sense if your existing rate is meaningfully above today's offers. The common rule of thumb from Bankrate and the lenders is that a refi tends to pay for itself if you can shave at least three quarters of a point to a full point off your rate and you'll stay in the home for five years or more. If you're already at, say, 6.5 percent or lower, you'd almost certainly be refinancing into a higher rate, which is a bad idea no matter what the Fed does next. If you're sitting on a 7.5 or 8 percent rate from 2023, the math could genuinely work in your favor, and the Fed's next move matters less than the gap between your rate and today's offer.

Also worth knowing: the Fed's own projections lean toward rates going up, not down, from here. Twelve of the officials surveyed expected another quarter‑point hike, and the committee's next decision is December 9 and 10. So waiting for a big drop that makes refinancing obvious isn't a great plan based on what's currently expected, though mortgage rates track 10‑year Treasury yields more than the Fed's short‑term rate, which is why the February cuts in 2024 and 2025 barely moved mortgages.
